$comment: Plain-words help for the navigator's "?" buttons (src/ui/explore/help.ts, help-popover.ts): loaded with their own chunk. Each should make sense to a curious young child: ordinary words, a simple picture where it helps, and true. Usually two or three short sentences.
help.navigator: This is your guide to space. Tap a world to fly there, and open the sections below to learn about it and try things out.
help.time: These buttons change time in the explorer: speed it up to watch the planets move, slow it down, run it backwards, pause it, or pick a date between 1600 and 2399. Outside JPL’s tables the Moon and planets come from published formulas, a little less exact. In an experiment they run its own clock, and backwards replays its history.
help.hijri: This is the date in the Islamic calendar, which follows the Moon: each month is about one Moon cycle. This one is worked out the way Saudi Arabia’s Umm al-Qura calendar does it.
help.orrery: A little map of the solar system seen from above, with the Sun in the middle. The directions are real for the date shown, but the distances are squeezed so everything fits.
help.distance: How far away each world is from you. An AU is the distance from the Earth to the Sun, about 150 million kilometres.
help.lightTime: Light is very fast, but space is enormous! This tells you how long light takes to reach you from each world. So looking far into space is also looking into the past.
help.seen: Special things you have noticed on this visit, like Jupiter’s squashed shape. It is just a list for you, not a score.
help.photo: Photo mode hides the buttons so you see only the view. You can save a picture or a video, with a note underneath of where its pictures and numbers came from.
help.detail: How much detail the explorer draws. More detail looks sharper but needs a faster device. Auto picks what suits yours.
help.sound: You hear the wind where there is air, like when you walk on the Earth or Mars. Where there is no air you only hear your space suit, because sound can’t travel through empty space. This also turns the film’s sounds on or off.
help.body.sun: The Sun is a star: a giant ball of very hot, glowing gas. About a million Earths could fit inside it, and its light and warmth keep us alive.
help.body.mercury: Mercury is the smallest planet and the closest to the Sun. It has almost no air, so its days are scorching and its nights are freezing.
help.body.venus: Venus is about the size of the Earth, but it is wrapped in thick clouds. Its air traps so much heat that it is the hottest planet, hotter even than Mercury.
help.body.earth: The Earth is our home: a rocky planet with air we can breathe and oceans of water. It is the only place we know of that has life.
help.body.moon: The Moon travels around the Earth about once a month. It has no air and no light of its own: it shines because sunlight bounces off it.
help.body.mars: Mars is a rocky planet about half as wide as the Earth. Its red colour comes from rusty dust, and it has the tallest volcano we know of, Olympus Mons.
help.body.jupiter: Jupiter is the biggest planet. It is made mostly of gas, so there is no solid ground to stand on, and its Great Red Spot is a storm wider than the Earth.
help.body.saturn: Saturn is a giant planet made mostly of gas, famous for its rings. The rings are countless pieces of ice and rock, all travelling around the planet.
help.body.uranus: Uranus is an icy giant planet. It is tipped over on its side, so it rolls around the Sun like a ball.
help.body.neptune: Neptune is the farthest planet from the Sun. It is an icy giant with the fastest winds of any planet.
help.radius: The radius is the distance from the middle of a ball to its outside. A bigger radius means a bigger world.
help.mass: Mass is how much stuff something is made of. A world with more mass pulls harder with its gravity.
help.density: Density is how tightly packed something is: a stone is denser than a sponge of the same size. Saturn is so light for its size that it would float in a giant bath of water!
help.gravity: Gravity is an invisible pull between things. It’s why you stay on the ground and why planets travel around the Sun. This number is how strong the pull is at the surface.
help.escape: Escape speed is how fast you would have to throw something straight up for it never to fall back. The stronger a world’s gravity, the faster you have to go.
help.day: A day is how long a world takes to spin around once. Here there are two: one full spin, and the time from one sunrise to the next, which can be quite different.
help.year: A year is how long a world takes to travel once around the Sun. Worlds farther from the Sun have longer years.
help.orbit: An orbit is the path something follows as it travels around another object. The Earth travels around the Sun, and the Moon travels around the Earth.
help.tilt: A world spins around a line called its axis. When the axis leans over, each half of the world gets more sunlight at a different time of year, and that makes the seasons.
help.fromSun: How far this world is from the Sun right now. Orbits are slightly stretched circles, so this distance changes a little through its year.
help.walk: Put on a space suit and walk on the ground! The shape of the ground comes from real measurements made by spacecraft.
help.descent: Ride down through the clouds the way a real space probe did. The numbers on the way down are the ones that probe measured.
help.sky: Lines and names you can add to the sky: the star patterns people have long known (constellations), their borders, and a grid that helps find places on the sky.
help.saved: Save the view you have now, with its place and date, so you can come back to it. Saved views stay in this browser only.
help.stars: Travel past the planets to the stars around the Sun. Each star is placed where telescopes measured it to be.
help.lab: This is where you can ask “What if?” about space. Change things like a planet’s mass or speed and see what the science models say would happen. It is a copy of the solar system: the real one is never changed.
help.living: The real Earth, live: today’s pictures from space, satellites going around it, and recent earthquakes. Turn on what you would like to see.
help.imagery: Choose the picture of the Earth: a clear one with no clouds, made from many photos, or today’s photo with today’s real clouds.
help.satellites: Satellites are machines people have sent up to travel around the Earth. Some take pictures, and some help phones and maps work.
help.quakes: An earthquake is when the ground suddenly shakes, because huge pieces of the Earth’s outer layer slip past each other. These marks show recent ones.
help.findPlace: Type the name of a town or city, then choose it to fly there.
help.fieldNotes: These are interesting places and things Samee wants to show you on the Earth. You can learn about them and visit the places in the explorer.
help.today: What is happening on the Earth right now: where the Sun is overhead, where the day is starting and ending, and where the space station is.
help.atlas: A tour of amazing places on the Earth, like great canyons, volcanoes and reefs. Tap Go to fly to one.
help.prophets: Places on the Earth linked by tradition to the lives of the prophets, peace be upon them. Where traditions disagree about a place, no pin is shown.
help.islamic: The Sun and the Moon help Muslims find the direction of prayer, the times of prayer and the start of each month. This section works these out with the explorer’s own astronomy.
help.qibla: The qibla is the direction Muslims face when they pray: towards the Kaaba in Makkah. Here it is the shortest path over the round Earth, measured from true north.
help.kaabaSun: Twice a year the Sun passes straight overhead at the Kaaba. At that moment the shadow of anything standing upright in the sunlit half of the world points away from the qibla, so a stick can show the way.
help.prayerTimes: Muslims pray five times a day, at times set by where the Sun is in the sky: dawn, midday, afternoon, sunset and night. Different organisations use slightly different rules, so you can choose one.
help.convention: Each organisation has its own rule for working out prayer times. They differ mostly in how far below the horizon the Sun must be for the dawn and night prayers.
help.asr: Asr, the afternoon prayer, begins when a stick’s shadow has grown longer than it was at midday: by the stick’s own length in one way of counting, by twice its length in another.
help.astrolabe: An astrolabe is an old instrument that shows the sky on a flat plate. Astronomers in the Islamic world used it to tell the time and find the stars. This one shows the sky for your place right now.
help.golden: The golden ratio is a special number, about 1.618, found in some shapes in nature and art. This shows how close the Kaaba’s latitude comes to the place that splits the way between the poles in that ratio: a closeness of numbers, not a proof of anything.
help.newMoon: At new moon the Moon is between the Earth and the Sun, so its lit side faces away and we can’t see it. A day or so later a thin crescent may appear after sunset, and many communities begin each Islamic month when it is seen.
help.crescentMap: This map shows where on the Earth the thin new crescent might be seen after sunset, from easily (green) to not at all (red). It shows what the sky allows, not when anyone’s month begins.
help.criterion: Astronomers have made tests, from many real sightings, to judge whether a new crescent can be seen. Yallop’s and Odeh’s are two of them, and you can compare them.
help.heritage: Places where great astronomers and mathematicians of the Islamic world lived and worked. Tap Go to visit them.
help.lightYear: A light year is how far light travels in a year: about 9.5 million million kilometres. A parsec is about 3.26 light years.
help.parallax: Telescopes find a star’s distance by watching it shift a tiny bit as the Earth goes around the Sun. It is like the way your finger seems to jump when you look at it with one eye and then the other.
help.spectralType: A star’s type tells you how hot it is and what colour it shines, from hot blue-white stars to cool red ones. The Sun is a yellow-white star of type G.
help.temperature: How hot the star’s glowing surface is, in kelvin (degrees above the coldest possible). The Sun’s surface is about 5,800 kelvin.
help.absoluteMagnitude: How bright the star would look if every star were set at the same distance. The smaller the number, the brighter the star really shines.
help.luminosity: How much light a star gives out in every direction, compared with the Sun.
help.apparentMagnitude: How bright the star looks from the Earth. The smaller the number, the brighter it looks: on a dark night the faintest stars you can see are about 6.
help.galaxyType: Galaxies come in different shapes: spirals like giant whirlpools, round or oval ones called ellipticals, and irregular ones with no clear shape.
help.hr: Each dot is a star, placed by its colour (left to right) and how brightly it really shines (up and down). Stars of the same kind gather together, like the long band where most stars, the Sun among them, are found.
help.exoplanets: Exoplanets are planets that go around other stars. Most are too faint to see: astronomers find them by the tiny wobble or dimming they cause in their star.
help.milkyWay: Our galaxy, the Milky Way, is a huge spinning disc of hundreds of billions of stars, and the Sun is one of them. This is a model of its shape, built from measurements.
help.localGroup: The Milky Way has neighbours: the Andromeda Galaxy and many smaller galaxies. Together they are called the Local Group.
help.cosmicWeb: Galaxies are not spread out evenly. They gather along huge threads and walls with great empty spaces between, like a web. These dots are real galaxies a survey measured.
help.starsSearch: Type a star’s name, like Sirius, or its catalogue number, then choose it to fly there.
help.walkGround: How high the ground is compared with the world’s “sea level”. On worlds with no seas, scientists choose a level to measure from instead.
help.walkGravity: How strongly you are pulled down here. On the Moon it is about a sixth of the Earth’s, so you could jump much higher.
help.walkAir: Air pressure is how hard the air above you presses down. On Mars the air is very thin, and on Venus it presses about 90 times harder than on the Earth.
help.walkSun: How high the Sun is in the sky, and the time a sundial here would show.
help.walkQibla: The direction of the qibla from where you are standing, and how far to turn to face it.
help.descentAir: How hard the air presses, how hot it is, and how thick it is at this height. Deep in Venus’s air it presses as hard as the sea does nearly a kilometre down.
help.descentProbe: These numbers were measured by a real probe that fell through these clouds, sending them home by radio as it went.
help.labClock: The laboratory’s own clock. Speed it up to see orbits and changes happen faster, or pause it to change things carefully.
help.labBodies: Everything in this experiment. Choose one to see its numbers and change them, and tick several to follow them together.
help.speed: How fast it is moving, and how fast compared with the world it travels around.
help.period: How long one trip around its orbit takes.
help.apsides: The nearest and farthest points of an orbit. Most orbits are stretched circles, so a world comes closer and goes farther as it travels.
help.eccentricity: How stretched an orbit is: 0 is a perfect circle, and the closer to 1, the longer and thinner the oval.
help.inclination: How tipped an orbit is compared with others, like a tilted hula hoop.
help.semiMajor: Half the longest width of an oval orbit: a way of saying how big the orbit is.
help.hill: The space around a world where its own gravity wins over the Sun’s, so moons can stay with it.
help.roche: If a moon comes closer than this to its planet, the planet’s pull is stronger on its near side than its far side and can pull it apart.
help.rotation: How fast it spins, and how far its axis leans compared with its orbit.
help.breakup: If it spun faster than this, the spinning would fling it apart, because its own gravity could no longer hold it together.
help.j2: How squashed a spinning world is. Fast-spinning worlds bulge out a little around their middle.
help.climate: How warm this world would be, worked out from its sunlight and its air. It is a simple model: it shows the big picture, not the weather.
help.sunlight: How much light from its star lands here, compared with how much reaches the Earth.
help.greenhouse: Some gases in the air trap heat like a blanket. More of them makes a world warmer.
help.push: A push changes how fast something moves and which way. A push along its path makes its orbit bigger, and a push against its path makes it smaller.
help.elements: These numbers describe an orbit: how big it is, how stretched and how tipped. Change them to put the body on a different path.
help.spin: How fast the world turns, and how much its axis leans.
help.fixed: Hold this body still, as if it were pinned in place, to see what happens to the others. Real worlds can’t be held still: this is a thought experiment.
help.prediction: The path drawn ahead is worked out by the computer from the same rules, a little way into the future. It is a calculation, not a certainty.
help.checks: These numbers check that the simulation is working properly. Energy and momentum should stay the same unless you change something.
help.history: Every change you make is listed here. You can go back to an earlier moment and try something different.
help.addBody: Add a new moon, planet or star to the experiment, and see how everything else responds.
help.ship: A spaceship with a rocket engine. Its fuel is limited, so every burn of the engine uses some of it up.
help.deltaV: Delta-v means “change in speed”. It tells you how much more speed the ship’s fuel can still give it.
help.burn: Which way the rocket pushes: forward along the path (prograde) makes the orbit bigger, backwards (retrograde) makes it smaller, and sideways tips it or changes its shape.
help.autopilot: The autopilot works out the burns for you, using the same rocket rules. It can only do what the fuel allows.
help.rings: Add a ring or belt of tiny pieces around a world and watch how gravity moves them.
help.frame: Choose how paths are drawn: around each world, as seen from far away, or turning along with a world. The motion is the same; only the view changes.
help.measure: Measure the distance between two objects, how long light takes to cross it, and the angle between them.
help.graph: Follow a number over time, like a distance or a speed, as a line on a chart.
help.lessons: Short guided experiments that show one idea at a time, with the number science expects beside the number the experiment gives.
help.camera: Settings for your picture: how wide the view is (the lens) and how bright it is (the exposure). You can also keep another world in the same place in the frame as time runs.
help.tour: Fly from one saved view to the next, like a little film. Record a video while it plays!
